subskill: identical objects shared with a minimum per person
template: identical pencils to three people / number of distributions / pre-allot the minimum, then share the remainder
method: Hand every person the required minimum first, then count the ways to share the few identical pencils that remain, remembering the pencils are identical so only the amounts matter.
prompt: Ten identical pencils are to be given out to Ava, Ben and Cara so that each of them receives at least 2 pencils and all ten pencils are given out. In how many different ways can this be done? (Two ways are different if at least one person receives a different number of pencils.)
explanation: Give each person 2 pencils first; 4 identical pencils remain to be shared among 3 people with no restriction. The amounts (a, b, c) with a + b + c = 4 are: (4,0,0) in 3 orders, (3,1,0) in 6 orders, (2,2,0) in 3 orders and (2,1,1) in 3 orders, for 3 + 6 + 3 + 3 = 15. The option "3" shares the 4 leftover pencils so that each person gets at least one more. The option "12" multiplies the 4 leftover pencils by the 3 people. The option "21" removes only 2 pencils in total before requiring at least 1 each (8 pencils, at least 1 each). The option "36" ignores the minimum of 2 and counts the ways in which each person gets at least 1.

subskill: probability that the greatest of several dice equals a value
template: three dice / P(greatest number is exactly 4) / at-most-4 minus at-most-3
mechanism: maximum equals k as difference of two at-most events
method: Count the rolls with every die at most 4 and remove the rolls with every die at most 3, since the greatest is exactly 4 precisely when all are at most 4 but not all are at most 3.
prompt: Three fair six-sided dice, each numbered 1 through 6, are rolled. What is the probability that the greatest of the three numbers showing is exactly 4?
explanation: The greatest number is exactly 4 when every die shows at most 4 but not every die shows at most 3: (4^3 - 3^3)/216 = (64 - 27)/216 = 37/216. The option "2/9" picks the die that shows 4 (3 ways) and lets the other two show anything up to 4 (16 ways), 48/216, counting rolls with two or three 4s more than once. The option "1/6" removes the rolls with two 4s once each (48 - 12 = 36) but forgets to add back the roll with three 4s. The option "61/216" is off by one, using (5^3 - 4^3)/216. The option "7/24" subtracts only the single roll 4, 4, 4 from the 64 rolls with every die at most 4, 63/216.
solve: var c=0; for(var a=1;a<=6;a++)for(var b=1;b<=6;b++)for(var d=1;d<=6;d++){if(Math.max(a,b,d)===4)c++;} return c/216;
interval: 216 equally likely rolls force a denominator dividing 216; all five options (216, 6, 9, 216, 24) do. The probability is below P(all at most 4) = 64/216; every option (36, 37, 48, 61, 63 over 216) is below it, none on it. It exceeds the single roll 4,4,4 (1/216); all options do.
bounds_checked: denominator dividing 216, upper bound P(all at most 4), lower bound one roll, monotone ladder (none: four different error paths), key/complement pairs (none)

mechanism: replacement changes the sum by new minus old
method: Turn the rise in the mean into a rise in the total, which equals the new number minus the number it replaced.
prompt: The mean of six numbers is 15. One of the six numbers is replaced by 31, and the mean of the six numbers becomes 17. What number was replaced?
explanation: The total rose from 6 x 15 = 90 to 6 x 17 = 102, an increase of 12. The new number exceeds the old one by 12, so the old number was 31 - 12 = 19. The option "12" is the increase in the total itself. The option "43" adds the increase to 31 instead of subtracting it. The option "14" subtracts the new mean from 31. The option "29" subtracts only the 2-point change in the mean from 31.

method: Count the four-digit numbers whose digits are all different, taking care that the first digit cannot be zero, and subtract that from the total number of four-digit numbers.

subskill: least possible size of a triple overlap
template: three overlapping groups in a survey / least possible number in all three / count the people missing from each group
mechanism: people outside at least one set
method: Count the people who are missing from each group; at most that many people can miss at least one group, so everyone else must be in all three.
prompt: In a survey of 100 people, 85 said they like apples, 75 said they like bananas and 60 said they like cherries. What is the least possible number of the people surveyed who like all three fruits?
explanation: 15 people do not like apples, 25 do not like bananas and 40 do not like cherries. At most 15 + 25 + 40 = 80 people fail to like at least one fruit, so at least 100 - 80 = 20 like all three, and 20 is reached when the three groups of non-likers do not overlap. The option "35" is the least overlap of just bananas and cherries (75 + 60 - 100). The option "45" is the least overlap of apples and cherries (85 + 60 - 100), treating a pair as if it were the triple. The option "15" counts the people who do not like apples, the smallest group missing a fruit. The option "80" is the greatest number who can miss at least one fruit, given as the answer.
solve: var N=100, s=[85,75,60]; var best=N; for(var t=0;t<=60;t++){ var miss=0; s.forEach(function(x){miss+=N-x;}); if(N-t<=miss){best=t;break;} } return best;
interval: The number is between 0 and 60 (the smallest group). 80 exceeds 60 and dies on that bound (one kill); 15, 35 and 45 lie strictly inside and survive. No option is on 0 or 60.
bounds_checked: part not exceeding the smallest group (60: kills 80), nonnegativity, key not the extreme on a least ask (15 lies below), arithmetic runs (none with the key in the middle), derivational hub (no option is double, half or one off the key)

subskill: probability one player reaches a smaller win target first in a series
template: series of independent games, unequal win targets / P(the player needing fewer wins takes the series) / extend the series to its full length
mechanism: imagine every possible game is played
at least k successes in a fixed number of trials
method: Notice that the series can last at most four games and that playing all four would never change the winner, so the series is won exactly when that player wins at least two of four independent games.
prompt: Ana and Ben play a series of games. In each game Ana wins with probability 1/3 and Ben wins with probability 2/3, there are no ties, and the games are independent. The series ends as soon as Ana has won 2 games or Ben has won 3 games. What is the probability that Ana wins the series?
explanation: At most 4 games are needed, and if all 4 were played the winner would not change: Ana wins the series exactly when she wins at least 2 of 4 games. P(0 wins) = (2/3)^4 = 16/81 and P(1 win) = 4 x (1/3)(2/3)^3 = 32/81, so P = 1 - 48/81 = 33/81 = 11/27. (Directly: WW 9/81, two orders of a 3-game win 12/81, three orders of a 4-game win 12/81.) The option "7/27" stops at 3 games, needing 2 wins out of 3 and forgetting the 4-game series. The option "29/81" counts only two of the three orders in which Ana wins in 4 games. The option "1/3" counts only one order of a 3-game win (9/81 + 6/81 + 12/81 = 27/81). The option "8/27" counts exactly 2 wins in 4 games, 6 x (1/9)(4/9).
solve: var c=0; var rec=function(a,b,p){ if(a===2){c+=p;return;} if(b===3) return; rec(a+1,b,p/3); rec(a,b+1,p*2/3); }; rec(0,0,1); return c;
interval: Every series outcome has probability a multiple of 1/81 (at most 4 games at 1/3 and 2/3), so the answer has a denominator dividing 81; all options (27, 27, 3, 81, 27) do. The probability is at least P(Ana wins the first two) = 1/9 and at most 1 - P(Ben wins the first three) = 19/27; every option lies strictly inside. Ana is weaker per game but needs fewer wins, so no direction relative to 1/3 or 1/2 is readable without the computation; options lie on both sides of 1/3.
bounds_checked: denominator dividing 81, lower bound 1/9 (absent), upper bound 19/27 (absent), naive per-game value 1/3 (a named error, not a bound), arithmetic runs with the key in the middle (none), key-is-sum, complement pair (16/27 absent)

The option "3/11" counts pairs with the SAME remainder (3 + 6 + 6 = 15). The option "32/55" counts each remainder-1/remainder-2 pair in both orders (32) over the 55 unordered pairs and leaves out the multiples of 3.

subskill: orders of 1-step and 2-step strides up a staircase
